note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Romaine is given a drawing to mark out a base plate. The drawing is revision C, but the job card says revision B. What should he do first?
options: Mark out from revision B, because the job card came first
Check with the supervisor which revision is current
Mark out from whichever copy shows the most sizes
Mark out from revision C and change the job card himself

questions.stem: A bracket drawing gives all sizes from the bottom edge and the left edge. The left edge of the plate supplied is flame cut and rough. What is the best way to mark out?
options: Measure from the rough edge and add 1 mm to each size
Ignore the drawing datums and mark from the plate centre
Mark from the right edge, because it looks straighter
Make a true datum edge or line first, then mark from it

questions.stem: A hole centre is given as 85 ± 0.2 mm from the datum. Which marked position is outside the tolerance?
Six holes are equally spaced on a 120 mm PCD (pitch circle diameter). What is the straight-line distance between the centres of two holes next to each other?
options: 40 mm
52 mm
60 mm
70 mm

questions.stem: Eight holes are equally spaced on a 200 mm PCD. You will step them off round the circle with dividers. What should the dividers be set to? (sin 22.5° = 0.383)
A hole is on a 100 mm PCD, 30° above the horizontal centre line. How far is it to the right of the vertical centre line? (cos 30° = 0.866, sin 30° = 0.5)
You mark a rectangle 1200 mm × 500 mm on a steel sheet. What should each diagonal measure if the corners are square?
Which tool gives the most accurate way to scribe a line at a set height above a surface plate?
options: A steel rule held upright against the work
A vernier height gauge with a hard scriber
A surface gauge set by eye to a tape measure
Odd-leg calipers run along the top of the work

questions.stem: Before a big marking out job, how should you check that a vernier height gauge reads correctly?
options: Check its zero on the surface plate and against a gauge block
Measure the height of the bench with a tape and compare
Scribe one line and check that it looks straight by eye
Wipe it with oil and read the scale against a steel rule

questions.stem: Why should heavy work be lowered gently onto a surface plate and never slid across it?
options: Sliding it would rub the marking blue off the work
The plate is only made for light work under 5 kg
Knocks and wear spoil the flat reference surface
The work could become magnetised by the plate

questions.stem: Holes must be marked on the face of a bracket that stands at 90° to its base. Which set-up on the surface plate is best?
options: Hold it upright by hand while you scribe
Clamp it to an angle plate and use the height gauge
Lay it flat and mark with a try square on its side
Stand it on vee blocks and mark with a steel rule

questions.stem: How do you mark a true centre line along the length of a round bar?
options: Hold the bar in a vice and draw along it with a rule
Mark the ends with a centre head and join them by eye
Lay it on the bench and scribe along a straight edge
Set it in vee blocks and scribe at its centre height

questions.stem: A drawing note says 'General tolerance ±0.5 mm unless stated'. One hole is dimensioned 40 ± 0.1. Which tolerance applies to that hole?
options: ±0.5 mm, as the general note always wins
±0.6 mm, the two tolerances added together
±0.3 mm, half way between the two
±0.1 mm, the tolerance stated on it

questions.stem: A hole position must be within ±0.05 mm. Why is marking out and centre punching alone not good enough?
options: The punch mark will rust before the hole is drilled
Hand marking cannot hold that; use a jig or machine set-up
A tolerance that small must be marked with a felt pen
The drill will always follow the punch mark exactly

questions.stem: You must mark out a plate with holes, slots and a shaped outline. What is the best order of work?
options: Punch every point first, then draw the lines between them
Mark the outline last, so that it can be cut first
Mark the datums, then centre lines, then features and outline
Mark the largest holes first, then the rest by eye

questions.stem: A template will be used to mark 40 gusset plates for a job in Old Harbour. What must be done before it is used?
options: Check it against the drawing and label it with the job
Paint it bright red so that it is easy to see in the shop
Use the first gusset cut as the template for the rest
Make it from card so that it is light and quick to handle

questions.stem: Why are templates for marking many parts usually made from steel sheet rather than card?
options: They are heavier, so they do not blow away
They keep their shape and hole positions over many uses
Steel templates can be bent to fit any shape of part
Card templates cannot have holes cut in them

questions.stem: A part will be flame cut from a marked line and then machined to its final size. Why is extra material left outside the finished line?
options: So the rough, heated edge can be machined off
So the part weighs more and is stronger in use
So the flame does not need to follow the line at all
So the drawing size can be changed later if needed

questions.stem: Five parts, each 380 mm long, are cut from one bar. Allow 3 mm for each of the five saw cuts. What length of bar is used?
Why should a centre punch mark be made lightly first, and checked, before it is made deeper?
options: So the punch does not go blunt too quickly
So the hammer does not bounce off the punch head
So it can still be corrected if it is off
So that the marking blue is not cracked

questions.stem: A light punch mark is about 0.5 mm off the crossing of two scribed lines. How can it be corrected?
options: Lean the punch to draw the mark over, then re-punch upright
Strike it much harder so that the drill wanders back
Fill it with weld and grind it flat, then start again
Leave it, because the drill will centre itself anyway

questions.stem: On a Level 3 job, who should check a large marked plate before any cutting starts?
options: Nobody, if the marker is experienced
The cutter, after the first cut is made
A second person, against the drawing
The customer, when the job is delivered

questions.stem: Why should the marker write the job number and part mark on each marked plate?
options: So that the plate can be sold later as scrap
So parts are not mixed up and can be traced
So that the marking blue sticks to the plate better
So that the cutter knows which saw blade to use

questions.stem: When marking holes in a steel angle, what is the 'back mark'?
options: The line scribed on the back of the flange to show the cut
The distance from the toe of the flange to the hole edge
A punch mark that shows the back of the part from the front
The distance from the heel to the line of hole centres

questions.stem: Kadeem must place a large, heavy plate on the marking table. What is the main manual handling control?
options: Lift it alone and quickly, to save time
Slide it off the edge of the rack by hand
Use a lifting aid or a planned team lift
Wear gloves only, as the weight is not a hazard

questions.stem: The marking blue (layout fluid) used at the Centre is a flammable liquid. What should be done?
options: Use it next to the welding bay so that it dries fast
Store it with the lid open so the fumes can escape
Pour any unused fluid down the drain at the sink
Keep it closed, away from flames; read the SDS

questions.stem: Tashana, a new trainee, is marking out under your lead. She measures each hole from the one before it. What should you do?
options: Show her how to work from the datum, and why
Let her finish, then re-mark the whole plate yourself
Tell her to work faster so the job does not run late
Give her a tape measure in place of the steel rule

questions.stem: You find that half the holes on a marked plate are 2 mm out because the wrong datum edge was used. What should you do?
options: Drill them anyway and open the holes later to fit
Cancel the wrong marks clearly and re-mark from the datum
Paint over the marks and pass it to the next shift
Mark the new holes beside the old ones, with no notes

questions.stem: How can you mark a straight line along a length of pipe, parallel to its centre line?
options: Wrap a tape round the pipe and mark a ring
Lay a piece of angle along it as a guide
Step off the radius with dividers along it
Draw it by eye while the pipe is turned slowly

questions.stem: How do you mark a square cut line all the way round a pipe?
options: Wrap a straight strip round it and scribe its edge
Use a try square at four points and join them by eye
Hold a steel rule across the end and scribe a line
Measure from the mill end, which is always square

questions.stem: Holes are needed at 75 mm pitch along a 900 mm edge, with the first and last holes 75 mm from each end. How many holes are there?
A slot is 12 mm wide and 40 mm long overall, with round ends. How far apart are the centres of the two end radii?
options: 40 mm
34 mm
28 mm
52 mm

questions.stem: Why should the Centre keep a record of when its height gauges and squares were last checked?
options: To work out the cost of each tool for the stores
To decide which trainees may borrow the tools
To meet the maker's warranty on the paintwork
To show they are still accurate enough to trust

questions.stem: A combination square is dropped on the concrete floor. What should be done before it is used again?
options: Keep using it as long as it does not look bent
Check it against a master square before use
Tighten the lock nut and carry on marking
Oil it well and put it back in its box

questions.stem: Before a bracket is welded onto a beam, the fitter marks the bracket's centre line on the beam. Why?
options: So its position can be set and checked after welding
So the welder knows what size of electrode to use
So the beam can be cut at that point if needed
So the paint shop knows which side to paint first

questions.stem: Holes in a welded frame must line up with bolts already set in a client's concrete base. Why are they often marked and drilled after welding?
options: Holes drilled before welding fill with spatter
Drilling is cheaper on a finished frame
Weld shrinkage can move parts out of position
Drawings never show holes before welding

questions.stem: The marking table is in a badly lit corner of the shop. Why is this a quality problem as well as a safety one?
options: Lines and scales are easier to misread
Marking blue will not dry in poor light
Steel expands when it is in the shade
Punch marks go deeper in poor light

questions.stem: A line is needed 25 mm in from a long, true edge of a plate, along its 2 m length. Which method is quick and accurate enough for ±0.5 mm?
options: Measure 25 mm at the middle only, then follow by eye
Set dividers to 25 mm and step along the line
Draw it freehand, then check it at both ends
Set odd-leg calipers to 25 mm and run them along

questions.stem: A line must be marked at 30° to a datum edge over a run of 200 mm. How far from the edge is the far end of the line? (tan 30° = 0.577)
Why is a circle the size of the hole often scribed round a centre punch mark?
options: So the hole can be cut with snips if needed
So the paint shop can find the hole later
So the driller can see if the drill drifts
So the punch mark does not rust over

questions.stem: You lead a team of four marking out parts for a gate in Linstead. How do you stop two people marking the same parts?
options: Let each person choose any parts they like
Give each person a part list and tick parts off when done
Mark all the parts yourself and let the others watch
Ask them to call out each part as it is finished

questions.stem: At the end of the shift the marking out is only half finished. What should the handover note say?
options: Which parts are marked and checked, and what is left
Only the time you finished and who was present
The tools you used, but not the parts marked
Nothing, as the next shift can see the plates

questions.stem: Why should a scribed line not be used on a polished stainless steel face that will be on show?
options: The scriber point will become magnetised
Stainless steel cannot be marked in any way
The scratch stays and spoils the finish
The line will turn to rust within an hour

questions.stem: A large steel square is found to be 1 mm out over 600 mm. What should the team leader do?
options: Use it only for long lines where it matters less
Bend it back by hand and use it again
Use it, and add 1 mm to every size
Take it out of use, tag it and report it

questions.stem: At the end of the job, what should be done with plates that are marked but not yet cut?
options: Stack them anywhere so they dry
Label them, store them flat and log them
Wipe off the marks so they look neat
Stand them against a wall, unsecured

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Name the tool, with a vernier or digital scale, that scribes lines at an exact height above a surface plate.
What is the name of the L-shaped cast iron block, with two faces at 90°, that work is clamped to on a surface plate?
Six holes are equally spaced on a 150 mm PCD. What is the distance, in millimetres, between the centres of two holes next to each other?
A drawing calls for four M12 tapped holes (coarse thread). What tapping drill size, in millimetres, is normally used?
A rectangle is marked 800 mm × 600 mm. What should each diagonal measure, in millimetres, if the corners are square?
What is the name of the hardened steel block of exact size used to check a height gauge or caliper?
What is the name of the accurate sheet pattern, checked against the drawing, used to mark out many parts of the same shape?
What do we call the distance between the centres of two holes next to each other in a row?
A hole centre is 30 mm to the right of and 40 mm above a datum corner. How far is it from the corner in a straight line, in millimetres?
What is the name of the small sliding scale on a caliper or height gauge that lets you read to a fraction of a millimetre, such as 0.02 mm?
Eight holes are equally spaced on a pitch circle. How many degrees apart are their centres, measured from the middle of the circle?
What is the name for the extra material left on a marked part so that it can later be machined to its final size?
What do we call a hole that has a thread cut inside it so that a bolt or set screw can be screwed in?
A hole centre must be 120 ± 0.3 mm from the datum. What is the largest distance, in millimetres, that is still acceptable?
What do we call a hole made longer in one direction than the bolt, so that a part can be adjusted when it is fitted?

essays.stem: You are the team leader for marking out 12 base plates, each with a shaped outline and four bolt holes, from one drawing. Explain how you would plan the job, share the work in your team and make sure every plate is right.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the drawing and the job card: revision, material, plate thickness, number of parts, sizes, tolerances and datums. I check that the plates in the store match, and that the marking tools are clean and recently checked. I plan the order: set up a datum on each plate, mark centre lines, then holes and outline, then punch. Because there are 12 the same, I would make one steel template, check it against the drawing, and get the supervisor to sign it off. I share the work: one person prepares and blues the plates, two mark out from the template, and one checks every plate with a rule and square against the drawing and ticks a check sheet. Each plate is marked with the job and part number. I check the first plate fully myself before the rest are done, and I check a sample during the job. At the end the check sheet goes with the plates to cutting.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing and job card: revision, material, sizes, tolerances, datums and quantity
Checks materials and tools before starting
Plans the order of marking (datum, centre lines, features, outline, punch) and uses a checked template for repeat parts
Gives clear roles to each team member, including a checker
First-off check, ongoing checks, part marks and a check sheet sent with the plates

essays.stem: A drawing gives sizes from two edges of a plate, but the plate supplied has rough flame-cut edges. Explain how you would set up datums for marking out, and why the choice matters.
essays.modelAnswer: A datum is the edge, line or point that all sizes are measured from, and it should match the datums the designer used on the drawing. A rough flame-cut edge is not straight or square, so measuring from it would put every feature out. I would either grind or file one edge straight and check it with a straight edge, or scribe a straight datum line just inside the rough edge, using a straight edge or a height gauge on the surface plate. I would then make a second datum at 90° to the first, checked with a large square or with the 3-4-5 rule. All sizes are then measured from these two datums, not from one feature to the next, so small errors do not add up. If the edges will be cut off later, I make sure there is enough material outside the finished line. Using the right datums means the parts will fit the mating parts and pass inspection.
markingPoints: Explains what a datum is and that it should match the drawing's datums
A rough edge must not be used: make a true edge or scribe a datum line
Sets a second datum at 90° and checks it (square or 3-4-5 / diagonals)
Measures all sizes from the datums so errors do not add up
Says why it matters: parts fit and pass inspection

essays.stem: Six holes are to be equally spaced on a 180 mm PCD on a round flange, with one hole on the vertical centre line. Explain, with your working, two ways to mark out the hole centres.
essays.modelAnswer: The holes are 360 ÷ 6 = 60° apart. Method 1, stepping off: the chord between holes next to each other is PCD × sin(180° ÷ 6) = 180 × 0.5 = 90 mm, which is the same as the radius. I scribe the 90 mm radius pitch circle from the punched centre, mark the top hole where the vertical centre line cuts the circle, then set the dividers to 90 mm and step round. The sixth step should land back on the first point; if not, I check the dividers. Method 2, coordinates: from the centre, the holes are at 90°, 30°, 330°, 270°, 210° and 150°. The top and bottom holes are at x = 0, y = ±90 mm. The other four are at x = ±90 × cos 30° = ±77.9 mm and y = ±90 × sin 30° = ±45 mm. I mark these from the centre lines with a height gauge. Finally I check the distance between holes next to each other, which should be 90 mm.
markingPoints: Works out the 60° spacing
Chord = PCD × sin(180° ÷ n) = 90 mm, stepped off with dividers from the top hole
Coordinates: (0, ±90) and (±77.9, ±45) from the centre lines
Marks from the centre lines with suitable tools (dividers, height gauge)
Checks the result: step closes on the first point, or chord measured

essays.stem: Compare marking out with a steel rule and scriber, with a combination set, and with a vernier height gauge on a surface plate. Say what kind of work each suits, and which you would choose for a machined bracket.
essays.modelAnswer: A steel rule and scriber are quick and need no set-up. They suit general fabrication work, such as cutting lines and hole positions with a tolerance of about half a millimetre or more, but the reading depends on the eye and can suffer from parallax. A combination set adds a square head, a protractor head and a centre head to the rule, so lines at 90° and 45°, angles and the centres of round bar can be marked quickly from a true edge. It is still read by eye from the rule, so it suits general work. A vernier or digital height gauge on a surface plate measures from a flat reference surface and can be set to a fraction of a millimetre. With an angle plate or vee blocks it can mark several faces from the same datum. It takes longer to set up but is the most accurate. For a machined bracket I would choose the height gauge and surface plate, because the tolerances are tighter.
markingPoints: Rule and scriber: quick, general work, accuracy limited by reading by eye
Combination set: square, angle and centre finding from a true edge
Height gauge on a surface plate: most accurate, set to a fraction of a millimetre, uses a flat reference
Mentions set-up aids (angle plate, vee blocks) or the time each takes
Chooses the height gauge for the machined bracket, with a reason

essays.stem: Describe how you would check that the main marking out tools (square, height gauge, steel rule and dividers or trammels) are accurate before a large job, and what you would do with a tool that fails.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check a square against the Centre's master square, or by marking a line, turning the square over and marking again from the same edge; the two lines must lie on top of each other. I would check the height gauge by zeroing it on a clean surface plate and then setting it on gauge blocks of known size. I would look at the steel rule for a worn or bent end and check it against a second rule or a tape known to be good. I would set the dividers or trammels against the rule, scribe an arc, measure it again and check that the points are sharp and the joint is firm. Every result is written in the tool record with the date. A tool that fails is taken out of use straight away, tagged 'Do not use' and reported to the supervisor or store keeper for repair or replacement, so that no one else picks it up.
markingPoints: Square checked against a master square or by the turn-over test
Height gauge zeroed on the surface plate and checked on gauge blocks
Rule checked for a worn or bent end; dividers or trammels checked against the rule
Results recorded with the date
Failed tool taken out of use, tagged and reported

essays.stem: Describe how to mark out a round steel bar for a hole drilled across it through its centre, and a flat for a set screw, using vee blocks and a height gauge.
essays.modelAnswer: I clean the bar and put marking blue on the end and along the area to be marked. I set the bar in a pair of vee blocks on the surface plate, clamped so it cannot roll. I measure the bar's diameter, and set the height gauge to the height of the centre: the height of the bottom of the bar above the plate plus half the diameter, or I find the centre with a centre head on the end. I scribe a centre line on the end face and along the side of the bar. I then turn the bar 90°, check the first line is upright with a square, and scribe a second line, so the cross on the end shows the centre. I mark the hole position along the bar from a datum end and scribe a short line across. For the flat, I set the height gauge to the depth of the flat below the top of the bar and scribe a line on the end and along the side. Finally I punch the hole centre lightly, check it and scribe a circle round it.
markingPoints: Cleans and blues the bar; sets it in vee blocks, clamped
Finds the centre height (bottom height plus half the diameter, or centre head)
Scribes the centre line, turns the bar 90° and checks with a square
Marks the hole position from a datum end and the depth line for the flat
Punches lightly, checks and scribes a guide circle

essays.stem: A job needs 50 identical gusset plates. Explain how you would make, check and control a marking template, and how you would check the parts marked from it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would make the template from thin steel sheet, not card, so it keeps its shape. I mark it out carefully from the drawing using datums, cut it and file it to the line, and drill the hole positions small enough to take a transfer punch. I check every size of the template against the drawing and get it checked and signed by the supervisor. I scratch or stamp the job number, part mark and drawing revision on it, and mark which side is the face, so it is not turned over by mistake. The template is kept in a set place and not used for any other job; if the drawing changes, it is checked again or replaced. When marking, the template is clamped to the plate against a datum edge. The first gusset is checked fully against the drawing. After that I check every tenth part, or as the job card says, and check the template itself for wear part way through.
markingPoints: Made of steel sheet and marked from the drawing's datums
Fully checked against the drawing and signed off before use
Labelled with job, part mark, revision and face side; stored and controlled
Clamped to a datum edge when used
First-off check, sample checks during the run and a check of the template for wear

essays.stem: Your team has three jobs: a cut line on a 3 m steel post (±2 mm), a bolt hole pattern on a base plate (±0.5 mm) and hole centres on a bracket that will be machined (±0.1 mm). Explain which marking out method and checks you would choose for each, and why.
essays.modelAnswer: The method should match the tolerance, so that time is not wasted on loose work and tight work is not spoiled. For the 3 m post at ±2 mm, a steel tape hooked on a squared end, a square and soapstone or a scribed line are enough. I would check the length again with the tape from the same end and check the line is square across all faces. For the base plate at ±0.5 mm, I would blue the plate, set up two datum edges at 90°, and mark the hole centres from the datums with a steel rule, combination square and scriber, then punch lightly. I would check the hole pitches and the diagonals of the hole pattern with a rule or caliper before final punching. For the bracket at ±0.1 mm, hand marking is not accurate enough to work to. I would mark it on a surface plate with a vernier height gauge, only as a guide, and the final hole positions would be set on the machine using its readout or a jig. I would check the first part with a caliper and record it.
markingPoints: Explains that the method is chosen to suit the tolerance
Post: tape from a squared end, square, re-check from the same end
Base plate: datums, rule, square and scriber, light punching, check pitches and diagonals
Bracket: height gauge on a surface plate as a guide; final positions set by machine or jig
Records or first-off checks for the tighter jobs

essays.stem: Describe the hazards when your team marks out heavy plate and long steel sections, and how you would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Heavy plate and long sections can cause back injuries and crushed hands or feet when they are lifted or turned. I control this by planning each lift, using a crane, hoist or plate clamp where we have one, using team lifts with one person giving the signals, and making sure everyone wears safety boots and gloves. Sharp edges and burrs can cut hands, so we wear gloves and deburr edges. Scribers and punches can stab or chip, so scribers are capped and punch heads that have mushroomed are ground back, and safety glasses are worn when punching. Marking blue and solvents can be flammable and give off fumes, so they are kept closed, used with good ventilation and away from hot work, as the SDS says. Long sections sticking out from the table are a trip and knock hazard, so they are supported on stands and marked. The area is kept tidy, with clear walkways and good lighting.
markingPoints: Manual handling: planned lifts, lifting aids or team lifts, boots and gloves
Sharp edges and burrs: gloves and deburring
Scribers and punches: capped points, dressed heads, safety glasses
Marking fluids: closed containers, ventilation, away from flames, SDS
Long sections supported and marked; tidy area, walkways and lighting

essays.stem: A batch of marked parts is found to have the holes in the wrong place. Describe what your report to the supervisor should contain, and say why each point matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The report should give the job number, drawing number and revision, and the part marks and number of parts affected, so the supervisor knows exactly what is wrong and where. It should say what was found and how: for example, that the hole centres were 2 mm out when checked against the drawing, and who found it. It should say how far the parts have gone, for example marked only, or already drilled, because that decides whether they can be re-marked or must be scrapped. It should give the likely cause, such as the wrong datum edge or a worn tool, so the same mistake is not made again. It should say what has been done already, such as stopping the batch, quarantining and labelling the parts, and taking the tool out of use. Finally it should suggest the next steps, such as re-marking from the right datum and re-checking, and give the date, time and my name. A clear written report keeps a record for quality checks.
markingPoints: Job, drawing, revision, part marks and quantity affected
What was found, how it was measured and by whom
How far the parts have gone (marked, cut, drilled), which decides rework or scrap
Likely cause and the action taken (stop, quarantine, tag tools)
Next steps, date, time and name, kept as a quality record

practical1.title: Plan, mark out and inspect a pipe flange plate with holes on a pitch circle
practical1.brief: As a team, plan and mark out a round flange plate from the drawing the assessor gives you, on 10 mm mild steel plate: an outside diameter of 220 mm, a centre bore of 90 mm and eight 18 mm bolt holes equally spaced on a 170 mm PCD, with two holes on the horizontal centre line. Before you start, write a short plan: the datums, the order of work, the tools and who does what. Work out the hole positions by two methods (stepping off and coordinates) and show the working on the plan. Each member marks at least one feature (centre lines, PCD and holes, outline, bore) while another member checks it. The team leader role changes half way. Punch the centres lightly, scribe guide circles, then punch witness marks on the outline. Fill in an inspection sheet with every size measured. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the plate and the sheet are finished and the area is clean.
materials: 10 mm mild steel plate, about 250 mm × 250 mm
Drawing of the flange (from the assessor)
Marking blue, scriber, centre punch, prick punch and ball pein hammer
Dividers, trammels or large dividers, steel rule and combination set
Surface plate or marking table, vernier height gauge and vernier caliper
Calculator, plan sheet and inspection sheet
photos: The written plan and the hole calculations
The plate cleaned and blued, with the centre lines scribed
The pitch circle and the eight hole centres marked
The hole centres punched, with guide circles scribed
The finished marking out with the outline witness-marked
A member checking a hole pitch, and the completed inspection sheet
checklist: Took part in writing the plan and can explain the datums and order of work
Worked out the hole positions correctly (chord about 65.1 mm, or coordinates from the centre lines)
Checked the tools before use and handled them correctly
Marked their feature accurately from the datum or centre lines
Punched lightly, checked and corrected marks before final punching
Checked another member's work against the drawing and recorded it on the inspection sheet
Led, or followed the leader's instructions, and communicated clearly
Wore the right PPE and left the area and tools clean and stored
safety: Wear safety glasses when punching; check punch heads and hammer heads before use
Keep scriber points capped when not in use
Wear gloves when handling the plate; lift it with a team lift or lifting aid
Keep marking blue closed and away from any hot work; follow the SDS
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Make and prove a marking template, then mark out a batch of gussets and angle cleats
practical2.brief: As a team, mark out parts for a small steel frame from the drawing the assessor gives you. First make a template for a triangular gusset (for example 150 mm × 150 mm with a 30 mm corner snipe and two 14 mm holes) from thin steel sheet. Check it against the drawing, label it with the job, part mark, revision and face side, and get the assessor to sign it off. Then use it to mark six gussets on 6 mm plate. Next, mark out four 50 × 50 × 6 mm angle cleats, 100 mm long, each with two holes on the back mark and pitch given on the drawing. Finally, mark a 1000 mm × 600 mm rectangle on a sheet and prove it square by its diagonals. Each member marks at least one gusset and one cleat, and checks parts marked by someone else. Record the first-off check and a sample check on the inspection sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the parts and the sheet are finished and the area is clean.
materials: Thin steel sheet for the template (about 1–1.5 mm)
6 mm mild steel plate for six gussets
50 × 50 × 6 mm steel angle, about 450 mm long
A sheet or board about 1100 mm × 700 mm
Marking blue, scribers, centre and transfer punches, hammer, clamps
Steel rule, tape, combination set, odd-leg calipers, large square
Drawing, inspection sheet and a calculator
photos: The template marked, cut and labelled, with the assessor's sign-off
The template clamped to a plate against a datum edge
The angle cleats with back mark lines and punched hole centres
The rectangle with both diagonals being measured
The completed inspection sheet with first-off and sample checks
checklist: Marked and checked the template against the drawing before using it
Clamped the template to a datum edge and transferred the shape and holes accurately
Marked the back mark and hole pitch on the angle correctly
Proved the rectangle square by measuring equal diagonals (about 1166 mm)
Labelled every part with the job and part mark
Checked another member's part and recorded the result
Shared the work fairly and followed the plan
Worked safely and left the area, tools and parts tidy and stored
safety: Wear gloves when handling sheet, plate and angle; deburr sharp edges
Support long pieces so they cannot fall or stick out into walkways
Keep marking blue closed and away from flames; follow the SDS
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
